pass_a_gloss: [...] portion of the Lord, his people Jacob, measured line of his inheritance Israel. Most terrible then it is to rise against the land of the Lord, that is, the Church, and to fulfil the daring deeds of bloodshed against the people allotted to Christ. For he will be in no way clean who is caught in charges so outlandish. But someone would say, I think, having considered the misfortunes upon Judaea and upon Jerusalem itself: Did the tyrant of the Babylonians come of his own accord, and march against the land of the Jews, and take the holy city, God not permitting him to do this, or rather not having given it to him? And yet the prophet Isaiah himself says to us that the Lord will whistle for the fly which rules part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee which is in the country of the Assyrians, and they will all come and rest in the ravines of the country, and in the holes of the rocks, and into the caves, and into every cleft, and on every tree. How then does the Babylonian, having served the nods [of God], have an inescapable charge, and is punished so terribly that nothing is seen beyond the anger brought upon him? Yes, and very fittingly. For the God of all wished to convict Israel, having turned aside to apostasy, and by measured afflictions to persuade him to run back to the worship customary to him, I mean that of the Law. But he, though brought for this, was implacable like a beast and used unbridled rages; and so he is charged, God saying clearly: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry at the nations that attack together; because I was angry a little, but they attacked together for evils. And as he raised up Pharaoh, being a vessel of anger and wrath and already subject to punishment for his own faults, as he himself says, so that he might show in him both his own power and the exactness of his just judgment, so you will understand also in the case of the Babylonians. For being vessels of wrath and owing to be punished justly, they were brought upon Jerusalem, so that having disciplined Israel they too after this might be required to pay the punishment most befitting and most suitable to them. [Lemma, Isaiah 14:20-22:] Wicked seed, prepare your children to be slaughtered for the sins of your father, so that they may not rise and fill the earth with wars. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord Sabaoth, and I will destroy their name and remnant and seed. Most terrible things Nebuchadnezzar did against every nation, and those after him and born of him, as far as Belshazzar, following the perversities of their father, leapt beyond his deeds, cruel and harsh [the section breaks off].

pass_b_english: …the Lord's portion is His people Jacob, Israel the measured lot of His inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9). It is therefore a most terrible thing to rise up against the land of the Lord, that is, the Church, and to carry out murderous outrages against the people allotted to Christ. For whoever is caught in such monstrous crimes will in no way be held guiltless.

But someone, I think, who has considered the calamities that befell Judaea and Jerusalem itself might say: “Did the tyrant of the Babylonians come of his own accord, march against the land of the Jews and take the holy city, without God letting him do it, or rather without God giving it to him? Yet the prophet Isaiah himself tells us: ‘The Lord will whistle for the fly that rules part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of the Assyrians, and they will all come and rest in the ravines of the land, and in the holes of the rocks, and in the caves, and in every cleft, and on every tree’ (Isaiah 7:18-19). How then can the Babylonian, who served God's command, bear a charge he cannot escape, and be punished so terribly that nothing can be seen beyond the wrath brought upon him?”

Yes, and with very good reason. For the God of all willed to rebuke Israel when he had turned aside to apostasy, and by measured chastisements to persuade him to run back to the worship he was used to, I mean the worship of the Law. But the Babylonian, though brought in for this purpose, was merciless like a wild beast and gave free rein to his fury. So he is accused, as God says plainly: “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that join in the attack; for I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack for evil” (Zechariah 1:14-15).

God raised up Pharaoh, who was a vessel of anger and wrath (Romans 9:22) and was already liable to punishment for his own offences, so that, as He Himself says, He might show in him His own power and the exactness of His just judgment (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16). In the same way you should understand the case of the Babylonians. They were vessels of wrath who justly deserved punishment, and they were brought against Jerusalem so that, after disciplining Israel, they too might afterward be given up to the punishment that most befitted and best suited them.

“Wicked seed, prepare your children to be slaughtered for the sins of your father, so that they may not rise up and fill the earth with wars. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will destroy their name and remnant and seed” (Isaiah 14:20-22).

choices.why: σχοίνισμα is land measured out by a line; Deuteronomy 32:9 speaks of Israel as God's own portion, not of God despising His people.
rejected: The Lord has despised his people Jacob

choices.why: νεῦμα is a nod of command; the objector says the Babylonian only carried out God's will.
The adjective describes the charge as one he cannot get out of.
θηρίου δίκην ἀμείλικτος: the Babylonian, not Israel, is the subject of the sentence.

choices.english: a vessel of anger and wrath
choices.why: Cyril draws on Romans 9:22; the vessel language is kept.
